utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe Mr. Mansfield had some points to raise, so I defer to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm most obliged. Your Honour, I would like to take one brief moment, if I might, as a matter of courtesy to you and the Tribunal to make an explanation and an apology, rather than for it be left without explanation, for those occasions when I'm unable to be here. I'm afraid there have been rather too many of those, I accept. The problem I'm afraid has been an ongoing one since 2003. I was engaged and am engaged in a major, long-running criminal case in London at the Old Bailey. The hearings began in 2003; however, without belabouring about how things became completely bogged down and derailed. The trial didn't begin when it was supposed to and it's now it's running about four or five months overdue over which I have no control whatsoever. I really apologise to you that occasionally I'm not able to be here; I have to be there. I'm not even in a position -- and I dare not, as you've discovered in these proceedings -- to make a prediction that it will end at the end of this month. It was supposed to have ended by the end of last year, but it still hasn't and there is evidence ongoing. I'm doing the best I can, and I'm sorry if that has not been understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, we are grateful for your explanation. We had not taken it as discourtesy. You had indicated that there were or was - I don't remember which - one or more conflicting interests which you were working your way through, and we fully understood that is the position. And fortunately you have left Mr. Khan to very ably keep the reins on behalf of your client, so we have been well assisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're ready to proceed with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you be good enough to read the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down, sir. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you understand me clearly and hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I realise I'm on the wrong channel. Sir, could you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Jakup Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I see that you have some papers that you have brought with you in front of you. Am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I have the right to possess some documents and I have brought with me some documents and materials that I think relate to this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I just want to ask you, just so we have a record, what it is that you have in front of you so that we're all clear about that.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have the statement I issued in Pristina to you and some statements issued by the General Staff of the KLA and a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I'm going to ask you, sir, is if you would, before you refer to any of those documents, if you would please let us know that you would like to refer to one of those documents. Do you understand what I'm saying? In other words, if you could put the documents to one side for now and I'll ask you questions, and if you have any difficulty answering any of my questions or any of the other questions that are put to you during your testimony, then perhaps you could ask to refer to one of those documents. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I may put them aside for the moment, and when I need them I will bring them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding. Now, sir, could you tell me your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: January the 1st, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was born in Fatos village, formerly Negrovce.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what municipality is that in?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is a rural municipality 30 kilometres west of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many years of education have you had?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Apart from the primary school, I finished the high school pedagogical school or faculty, and post-university studies in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you finished your education, your schooling, your education, did you start working?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you did at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I used to do two jobs. I worked in the educational system. I worked in a primary and in a high school. I was a member of clandestine organisations which we called illegal or secret organisations against the occupier, the former Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about each of those jobs, but let me start with your work in the educational system. Were you a teacher in the primary and high school?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was also a teacher in the primary school and in the high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how many years did you do that? How many years were you a teacher?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I wasn't lucky to work very long as a teacher. I worked during the studies and a little after the studies, because in April 1981, I was imprisoned by the former Belgrade regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us where you were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was imprisoned in Pristina of course, and I did a sentence of ten years and four months from April the 5th, 1981, until 23rd July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the reason that was given for imposing that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In 1980/1981 in Kosova a movement was organised, a clandestine and a student movement, which was transformed into a popular movement. The demand of this movement was for Kosova to become a republic in the Yugoslav federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Is that -- was it because of your participation in that movement that you were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I said I was member of its organisation, but I also participated in all the demonstrations that were staged in Pristina in the spring of 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if you remember, Mr. Krasniqi, what was the actual charge that the Serbs said was the reason for your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The reason -- the indictment was, under the Yugoslav law, activity -- counter-revolutionary and hostile activity. It was interpreted under two articles, 214 and 226.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krasniqi, you told us that in addition to teaching you had joined some clandestine organises and I think you've already provided a little bit of information about that. But can you tell us specifically when did you join these organisations? What year?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was -- joined one organisation and this happened in 1973. Might be early 1974 probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the name of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That organisation was called Marxist-Leninist Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you a member of that organisation from the time you joined until the time you were imprisoned in 1981?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you were released from prison in 1991, ten years later, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After I was released, I engaged in political activities. At that time in Kosova there was a democratic alternative movement in place and I was a member of the Democratic League for the Drenoc local branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you lived in Kosovo your entire life or have you lived for periods of time outside of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: With the exception of the time I was in prison, and this was outside Kosova, I have lived mainly in Kosova. During the war in the last month after my return from Rambouillet and Paris conferences, I was for some months in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the last question on this topic: You said you were imprisoned outside of Kosovo. Where was that? Someplace in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was in several prisons but most of my term I did in Zrenjanin and Novi Sad, in the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic, but before I do that I want to ask you some questions about your appearance here today. Did you receive a subpoena from the Court to appear here today?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive a subpoena, and I want to declare here in the presence of Their Honours that initially I stated that I am not willing to testify against Fatmir Limaj and his comrades. This was one reason. The other reason was that even today I believe that the Kosova Liberation Army during its short existence and life didn't commit crimes for which it's being accused, and I don't see any reasons for its members to be put here in The Hague Tribunal. I didn't want to issue statements. My statements have been always public, transparent in the eyes of the Kosova and international public, and I didn't have more to add to them. The duty of a spokesperson in every army in every country are known. And another reason is that to this day I believe that the indictment against the three accused has been built on politically motivated evidence given by the people who have been in the service of the violence of the occupiers in Kosova. I am a witness that they have been processed in advance. Before they were given to the investigators of the Tribunal, they have been processed by the Serb intelligence service. These were the reasons for my hesitation to appear here in the court and to issue statements to the prosecutors. That's why I refused to come of my own free will, even though I have a lot to say, especially about the political struggle of the Kosovo Liberation Army. And before the Tribunal today I'm going to tell the truth regarding the KLA, its just and liberation struggle which was in fact waged by the people of Kosova; the KLA just led the struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Krasniqi, all I ask of you is that you answer my questions and tell the truth. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Even now I said the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. And it is -- so -- just so I understand your answer there, it's in compliance with the subpoena that you are here today. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I already stated my reasons for my hesitation, but still I am here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Now, sir, on April 27th of 2004, did you attend an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor in Pristina pursuant to a summons from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. And at that time I have told you and there is a document here, point 4, that I intend to be a witness for the Defence lawyers of Mr. Fatmir Limaj, and for these reasons I refuse to be a witness for the Prosecution. This is what I told you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. And what you've just referred to when you said "point 4" is the report of the interview that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor on April 27th, 2004. Is that right? Just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in that interview on April 27th, 2004, were you truthful?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I was truthful in regard to what I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after the interview, did you later learn that the recording equipment at the interview had malfunctioned and that there was no tape of the interview? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I learned that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And on the 21st of June, 2004 - I understand if you don't remember the exact date but you can -- I believe it was on that date - were you given a report of the questions and answers at the interview in the Albanian language? And did you have an opportunity to review that report and then on the following day initial and sign the report?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, but the report was not built or written on the basis of a recorded tape, but it was written on the basis of the notes taken by your staff during that time. This is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's -- thank you for that clarification; that's correct. My next question is: When you -- I understand that it was a -- not a verbatim report of what had occurred at the interview, it was a summary of what had occurred at the interview. But when you initialled each page and signed it, were you agreeing to the accuracy of the summary of what had occurred at the interview?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In general it was what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, when did you join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We have to divide that -- the existence of the KLA in two parts. It has -- it's composed of the political leadership, which of course has the operational aspect or side. From the beginning, from the inception of the KLA, together with the other comrades that formed this KLA, I was there. We were organised in the political bodies which then did not have the name KLA even before 1991. It was -- to be precise, in 1991 it celebrated its 30th anniversary when Adem Jashari and the armed political formation in Prekaz put up the first armed resistance against the Serb police and military forces. Then with its political formation, Adem Jashari was for some days at my family, then he stayed with some other families in my village. And this is how we began to link up with the armed wing and in 1993 I may say that the KLA was formed as such, which at a later time in 1994 through its communiques would become known to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you some more -- some further questions about what you just told, but I realise I neglected to ask you an important question. That is: How are you presently employed?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Presently I am the general secretary of the Democratic Party in Kosova and the chairman of the parliamentary group of this party in the Kosova parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Democratic Party in Kosovo, is that known by its initials, the PDK?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so I understand your answer, you are a member of parliament and you are in fact the chairman of the parliamentary group of your party in the parliament. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were you until recently a member of the government, a minister in the government?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. In the first legislature, I was Minister of Public Works in the Kosova government, provisional government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was from what year to what year?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This was from March the 4th, 2002, until 1 December 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was it because there was a change in the government that you are no longer in that position?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There are -- naturally there are changes in the government and my party is in opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to the answer you gave a few moments ago about the beginning -- about your beginning involvement in the KLA and just make sure I understand what you were telling us. Do I understand that in 1991 you joined -- the political organisation that you joined was in some senses a precursor to the KLA. Is that what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It's not exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, please explain.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I said earlier that on July 23rd, 1991, I was released from jail after ten years and three, four months. I was a member then and in Kosova there existed a greater party, a democratic party -- Democratic League. Since most of the citizens had subscribed to that movement and party, even though people referred to it more as a movement, would be most seriously committed to the realisation of the aspirations of the Kosova citizens, so that they, too, enjoy freedom and democracy - meaning I was a member of the Democratic League then. But during this time an armed action was undertaken. These actions were naturally the -- were organised in -- underground. So this was the beginning of the armed resistance, which I described also as part of my struggle in a political plain to implement the aspirations of Kosova citizens, freedom and democracy; to help them build their independent state; to ensure the freedom of all its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when would you say that you joined the armed struggle? When was that? What year was that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I already said that we may say that 1993 marks, in a way, the unification of the political wing and the armed wing. And from this unification, I would say -- this unification resulted in the emergence of the KLA, which in 1994 through a communique made public that due to the severe Serb repression and violence, maltreatment, and constant persecution of Albanians, due to violence, savage violence exercised by the occupier in Kosova, which had been doing that even earlier in the Milosevic time, it stepped up this violence, becoming unbearable for the population. Under such circumstances, they formed the political and military formation which was now known by the name of Kosova Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when that occurred in 1993/1994, did you think of yourself as being in the -- I understand that these two wings merged, the political wing and the armed wing. After 1993 and 1994, were you in the political wing or in the armed wing? Or were you in both?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was more in the political wing because I was in Kosova and during all that time I was there I was also a member of the Presidency of the Democratic League in Drenoc. I was also a member, a deputy, because in 1992 in Kosova we held free elections. And during those elections, I was elected as the deputy for Drenoc in the Kosova parliament, a parliament which due to the repression and the violence and the obstacles put to it by the Belgrade regime never managed to appropriately constitute itself and function as a proper parliament. At the same time -- this was my legal activity but there was also the underground activity. Because at that time to fight for democracy was forbidden under the laws of the Yugoslav federation, which now actually had -- then become the laws of Serbia, which kept only the name as the Yugoslav federation. So to work for our country, it was necessary for us to engage in illegal, clandestine organisations. I don't know which word would suit better your vocabulary, but it boils down to the same thing. They were secret organisations because we did not have other possibilities to act. That's why my being in the KLA initially illegally and then my legal presence in the LDK was a must. I never accepted being debased by the Belgrade regime or the debasement that this regime made of most of the citizens in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, can you briefly tell us what the illegal or clandestine activities comprised of. What was that? You've told us what the political activity was; what was the illegal, clandestine activity at this time, 1993/1994?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The illegal activity aimed at expanding the resistance wing in Kosova on a national level. They aimed at preparing the citizens of Kosova to -- for the liberation war. They aimed that the violence and Serb terror be halted. They aimed that the Kosovar citizens regained their dignity and honour, their freedom, independence and democracy. That was the aim of this organisation and all the other organisations in Kosova following the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've described what the aims or goals of the illegal and clandestine activity were. Now -- briefly, what was the means? What means did you use to attempt to achieve those goals?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In 1991 the citizens of Kosova had exhausted all the political means of war. So the only means left to them was to engage -- to create armed formations for them to realise their freedom and democracy against those who were engaged in violence and terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, in 1993 and 1994 did you yourself participate or engage in armed formations?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't take part personally in such formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you did?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have always been the -- a member of the political wing in the Kosova Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, before I move on to later dates, at this time in 1991 did the LDK exist in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. It was formed in around December 1990/1991, meaning that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were you yourself a member of the LDK in addition to being a member of the Democratic League?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: But the LDK and the Democratic League are one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when you broke from the LDK, when you stopped being a member of the LDK?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell me what year that was.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This happened in 1998 when I saw that the path followed or chosen to be followed by the LDK was a path that didn't lead anywhere. Over 400.000 people had left Kosova while terror or cleansing was being pursued in Kosova. The people were being maltreated from all sides. Every main street -- In all the roads of Kosova you could see police roadblocks and checkpoints where all the citizens of Kosova without exception were being maltreated with the purpose of -- for these citizens not to feel at home in Kosova but to flee it and that Belgrade regime could re-colonise Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, we will talk certainly more about these issues later, but I just at this point want to ask you this: What month in 1998 did you break from the LDK for the reasons you've just described? What month was it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I became displeased with the KLA -- sorry, with the LDK at the end of 1997 and beginning of 1998, especially following the event of 28 February 1998 and that of 5, 6, and 8 March 1998. That was the moment when I broke away from the policy followed by the policy of silence and doing nothing of the LDK. And it was then that I passed on to the Kosova Liberation Army quite openly. I broke away from them really on the 3rd and 4th of March, 1994, on the occasion of the burial ceremony of the 14 victims of the Serb terror. It was at that time that I gave a political speech there which marked my open, official breaking away with that party, with which its policy had become an obstacle for the Kosova people to realise their freedom and democracy and independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I think we had a little problem with the translation so I'm going to ask you this question. You said you broke with them on the 3 and 4th of March, and I believe you intended to say to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say March 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've heard some testimony about this and I think everybody in the courtroom is familiar with what occurred on these dates, the 28th of February and the 5th and 6th of March. But just so the record is clear and your testimony is complete, could you briefly tell us what it was that occurred on those dates.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is 5, 6, 7, and 8 March.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is it that occurred on those dates, the 28th of February and those dates in March in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I was still the chairman of the Drenoc LDK branch legally or officially. And I followed closely on a daily basis the political developments that occurred in Drenoc commune -- municipality, which is one of the two municipalities of Drenica. On that day large military and police Serb forces attacked several villages of Drenica, of the north-eastern part of Drenica. And at that time we couldn't know -- it was not possible for us to know what was the goal of these force -- of such large presence of forces in that area in those villages, Likoshan, Granacell and Qirez.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you've given a partial answer to my next question but I want to give you an opportunity to address it more completely, though briefly, if you could. And that is: What was it about those events that occurred at the end of February and beginning of March 1998 that caused you to be disenchanted with the policies of the LDK? Can you explain that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This happened mainly because of the terror and genocide that were being committed by the Belgrade regime in Kosova. It was at this time that two events, painful events not only for the Albanians and for Kosova, happened. This happened in Likoshan and Qirez where the Serb military police and paramilitaries in a day killed 14 people 11 of whom were unarmed, people who the police and the army found in their homes. Among the victims was also a pregnant woman. And to further clarify this point I want to say that if [as interpreted] on the 28th of November, 1997, in Llausha, we buried a teacher killed by the Serb army which was attended by 20.000 people. In the burial of these victims on the 28th February and the 1st of March, 1998, and on -- 3 and 4 March, 1998, in Likoshan which was attended by over 200.000 people, this shows how much the discontent -- how great was the discontent of the population of Kosova at the policy followed by the Belgrade regime. So at the funeral of the teacher in Drenica, as I said, was attended by 20.000 people. The funeral at Likoshan and Qirez were attended by over 200.000 people, in a word --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, if I can direct you a little bit in your answer. I understand what you've told us about the events on these dates. If you could just tell us: What was it that then -- what was it about these events that caused you to be disenchanted with the LDK? Because I believe that's what was your testimony. But what was about these events that caused that? Why did you become disenchanted with the LDK when these events happened?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I already said that the LDK didn't represent anymore the interests and the voice of the Kosova citizens. So it was necessary for somebody else to become the torch-bearer of the interests of the Kosova citizens. Someone had to stop the Serb genocide in Kosova and this is what the people expected the KLA to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to be patient with my questions because I know you know this information very well and some of my questions may seem obvious, but we need to have clarity about these issues. So can you explain for us what was the difference of the approach of the LDK and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I believe that the differences, for the Trial Chamber and all of you, are known. The LDK was not engaged in a movement to do away with the Serb violence in Kosova. In one way or another it had become a stooge of this regime, to -- to deprive the rights of the Albanian people to live in peace and freedom and independence and democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say that the LDK had become a stooge of the regime, I assume you're talking of the Serb regime. Did -- are you saying that the LDK generally adopted a passive approach to resistance?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Both. The LDK was engaged in a very passive resistance and didn't move things. It was a movement that hoped that someone from the sky would bring freedom and democracy. It was, in my opinion, a vain expectation. We had been waiting for that for 50 years, hoping that Yugoslavia would understand that we needed our rights for almost 90 years it has ruled in Kosova. It has been unable of building a public, democratic administration that was accepted to its citizens. So it was in vain to wait any longer for a regime -- from a regime that had destroyed the entire Yugoslavia when it was led by a dictator that the Tribunal knows very well. I don't want to mention even his name here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: And the fight against that regime had become inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so just so I'm sure I understand your testimony, the KLA proposed that as an alternative, armed active resistance to the Serb regime? Am I understanding your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. But maybe we have to go back a little bit in time. You know that in 1995 there was a conference held in Dayton regarding the Yugoslav federation. And in that conference where Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina took part, which had been fighting against Milosevic people, Kosova was not invited even though Kosova was also engaged in a passive resistance. And the voice of this resistance was not heard. In Dayton, either -- then the LDK chairman used to say that we didn't take part in Dayton, but we are going to take part in London, Paris, and Moscow and in similar conferences, which was not the case. So only those who created new realities in their own respective countries participated in Dayton. So for the KLA it was clear that a new reality had to be created in Kosova for the international community to take into consideration the just demands for freedom, democracy, and an independence of the Kosova citizens. This is why, following Dayton, the KLA enhanced its organisation in both wings, the military and the political ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When the Kosovo question was not addressed at Dayton, did more people in Kosovo begin to look for an alternative to the LDK and start to turn to the KLA? Do you understand my question? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. All the developments in 1996 and also in 1997/1998 go to prove that the citizens of Kosova were deflecting from the passive resistance. They were tired from violence, repression. And there were only two ways left to them, either to fight in Kosova or to flee Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you've referred to the LDK chairman who said after Dayton that the Kosova question would be addressed elsewhere in London, Paris, or Moscow. Was that LDK chairman, was that Mr. Rugova, Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chairman, but I want to be precise in one issue. Our organisation in war was not meant to oppose LDK or Kosova, it was meant to fight the Serb occupier, which -- and the repression which reached its height during the time of the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time that you became a member of the General Staff of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that, please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It might have been end of 1996 and beginning of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us who else was on the General Staff of the KLA at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. If you want this issue to go down in history, I can give names, of course, because these people have names and last names. I have to say one thing before the Trial Chamber. The organisation was a clandestine one. It was an underground form of organisation and at that time not everyone -- I didn't know everyone, as the others didn't know me, not all of them did, because of the position I held at that time in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the other people on the General Staff as you knew them?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. The General Staff during that time was spread out in three parts. One part operated in Kosova, underground. Another part -- it was a minority probably, this lived in Albania outside Kosova. And another part lived and worked in the western countries; in Switzerland, Germany, the United States, in France, in the Scandinavian countries. We were, as I said, spread out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And the part that was in Kosova underground was obviously the part you were in. And can you tell us who else was in that part?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. It is known now that commander of the KLA at that time was Adem Jashari. Sokol Bashota was there, Rexhep Selimi, while several others, as I said, were abroad as in Albania and different countries in the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know the names, either as pseudonym or as true name of any of the others who were abroad?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know them and I think that neither them [as interpreted] knew my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it came about that you joined the General Staff. How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I already said that from the beginning, from December 1991, I had contacts with the commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army, which at that time of course was not Kosovo Liberation Army but it was in the form of that two wings, the political wing and the military wing. Then in 1993 in March or April 1993, there was a meeting between several representatives of the political wing with the informations of the Adem Jashari in his house in the village of Prekaz, Skenderaj municipality and here we divided the duties between us. Some were engaged in the operations level and some on the political level. I was amongst those engaged on the political level. I was in the directorate of the political wing of the KLA where Hashim Thaqi was the chairman. Adem Jashari and his formations were part of the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to be clear in December -- you said you had contacts with the commander of what would become the Kosovo Liberation Army in December of 1991. Are you speaking about Adem Jashari?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now you've explained how it is that you joined the KLA, we'll call it, in March/April 1993 and you became engaged in the political activities. When you -- how did it come about that you joined the General Staff at the end of 1996 or beginning of 1997? How did that happen? Were you asked? Was there some other procedure?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We should understand here that the beginnings of the KLA organisation were not of a formation which could freely exercise their duties. It was an organisation that had to exercise its activity secretly because the Belgrade regime had installed many police and army forces in Kosova, uniformed ones. This regime also had at its disposal many forces within the secret service, so it wasn't easy at all to organise oneself into illegal operations and operate. These were difficult times and conditions, and it wasn't preferred at that time to deal with documents and papers in writing because this at that time was a risk. It was a sort of idealism for these people who were organising and a determination to operate. So if you're now looking for procedures of armies operating in legal conditions with budgetary and infrastructure regulations, we can freely say that this did not happen in Kosovo and it wasn't possible to happen in such administrative forms and shapes as it is in countries where people live freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm sorry -- I just -- I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I want to focus a little bit here. I understand your explanation that the -- that there were no written documents and that things operated secretly. But my question just was: How was you became a member of the General Staff? Because you told us you became a member of the General Staff at the end of 1996, beginning of 1997. And I just was asking, how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I would like to explain this one more time that my contacts with both the wings, both the military and army wing -- sorry, military and political wing existed from 1991. As for the political part, I explained earlier that I was in the political activity since 1973 and spent over ten years in prison because of that activity. Politically I was organised even early before the KLA came into service --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sorry, I would like to explain this to the Trial Chamber. In 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll give you an opportunity to explain it, I will. I just think you've perhaps misunderstood my question or I've put it poorly. My question was really: Did somebody ask you -- not what your experience was that led up to becoming a member of the General Staff, it just was -- it actually was more simple than that. Did somebody ask you to become a member of the General Staff? Were you elected? Did you ask, yourself, to become a member of the General Staff? What happened at the time? What happened at the end of 1996, beginning of 1997 that caused you to become a member of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In 1996 and 1997 we mentioned the Dayton conference, the political circumstances changed, not only Kosovo but in the entire territory of the former Yugoslav federation. Changes occurred in Kosovo as well. I was not earlier appointed member of the General Staff because I was already in Kosovo. And as I said, this activity was mostly taking part abroad and on individual basis. In 1996, the need for expansion of the activity of the KLA in Kosovo emerged. Of course this consulting did not occur only between us; we had our representatives abroad and we all agreed to increase the military and political activity in Kosova. In such circumstances we discussed with comrades with whom I constantly maintained contact from 1993 and earlier, and as I said I had to engage more in Kosovo because I was there in the military and political expansion of the KLA in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: And in the end of 1996, beginning of 1997 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I'll let -- let me pose this question to you: Who -- you said you were appointed to be a member of the General Staff. Who appointed you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army, Adem Jashari.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned Hashim Thaqi. Was he also a member of the General Staff at this time? And we're talking end of 1996, beginning of 1997.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And at this time, at the end of 1996, beginning of 1997, did the General Staff meet on a regular basis or how would you communicate with other members of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We would meet quite rarely, due to security reasons. We would consult through electronic means, by electronic means, because majority of comrades were outside of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you say you met rarely. How -- can you give us an idea how often? Was it once a week? Once a month? Less frequently than that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This depended on the political development. Sometimes we would not meet for months and sometimes we would meet often, very often, due to the circumstances. In other words, there wasn't a regular pattern when we would meet. I would stress again that this was depending on the political developments in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say you communicated at times through electronic means, including with people -- members outside of Kosovo, what do you mean exactly by electronic means? Can you explain that? Is that by telephone or some other ...

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: By phone, by fax, and other forms as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Now, did you -- I'm going to move us forward in time to the spring of 1998. At that time were you still a member of the General Staff? And just to be more precise, the spring of 1998, we'll say May of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was even before May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. But in May of 1998 you were still a member of the General Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In May 1998, in June, and continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And at that time, in May or June of 1998, can you tell us who else was a member of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Again, during this time not all members of the General Staff were in Kosova. Now, after the March events the general commander of the KLA in Kosova was Azem Sula. Deputy commander was Sokol Bashota. General inspector was Rexhep Selimi. And other members of this staff at this time were myself, Llahib Rrahimi [as interpreted]. Xhavid Zeka was not there. Xhavid Haliti was not inside, but he was a member of the General Staff. Hashim Thaqi and Kadri Veseli.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where was Xhavid Haliti? You say he was not inside. Where was he?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Xhavid Haliti, yes. He was within this staff but he lived in Albania. He did not live in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, on the 11th of June, 1998, were you appointed to a particular position in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I then assumed the position of the spokesperson to convey the policy of the Kosova Liberation Army to the public opinion within Kosova and abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the usher I'm going to put before you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I actually ask that a binder be placed before the witness. Your Honours and the parties have been provided with this binder. I'm going to ask the usher, please, to assist the witness and turn to tab 2. And for the record tab 2 is Prosecution Exhibit P49, while the rest of us will turn to tab 1, which is Prosecution Exhibit P48. And in tab 2 if the witness could be shown -- it's ERN U008-1630. And in the English, tab 1, it's U003-8575. And it's also on the Sanction, should be on the computer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm putting before you a page from the newspaper Pristina Bujku, it's from the 12th of June, 1998, and it's page 5. I want to draw your attention to the top right of the page. I'm sure you've found it there. And the rest of us have a translation of that article. Now, I see that you've pulled out a piece of paper there.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This is the same thing, just enlarged here where I sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I actually -- I understand because the copy that you have is actually quite small and I've asked Mr. Younis to have prepared and I should have put it in front of you. I have a large version of it because in fact this is from a newspaper. That should be easier. Why don't -- we'll refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if the usher could again find the page, it's 1630, U008-1630. And just for the record, this paper that we've put before the witness is the same exhibit, just larger. P49. And this should be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, again, I draw your attention to the article at the top right -- and specifically to the end where it says: "The UCK General Staff has decided to appoint Professor Jakup Krasniqi as its spokesman. Professor Jakup Krasniqi was born on 1 January 1951 in the village of Negroc in Drenice, where he still lives." And it's signed the General Staff of the Kosovo Liberation Army, Pristina, 11 June 1998. And sir, was that in fact your announcement of your appointment to be spokesman in fact issued by the General Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell us what your responsibilities were in this position. I think you've already given a little bit of an answer to this question, but what were your duties as spokesman of the KLA as you understood them?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier what was the duty of the KLA spokesperson. I believe that many here know very well the duties of a spokesperson. My duty was communication with the media so that the KLA before the media in Kosova and those of the western countries and the United States that were largely present in Kosova at that time, my duty was to present before the public opinion the political programme of the Kosova Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that position?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I held this position until the formation of the provisional government of Kosovo after the Rambouillet conference. And in the early beginnings of the provisional government I was still a spokesperson until June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the Rambouillet conference was in what month and year?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It consisted of two parts. The first part occurred in Rambouillet in February 1999 and the second part in Paris in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. We will now have a break. You've been giving evidence for nearly an hour and a half, so a break will assist you. It's also necessary for technical reasons, as the tapes have to be changed over. We will resume sitting at 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when you became a member of the General Staff at the end of 1996 or beginning of 1997, I believe that you referred to communiques from the General Staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I mentioned the communiques even earlier. As of 1994 we started to issue some communiques to inform the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were the communiques issued by the General Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Most of them were issued by the General Staff. They have informed the public of the activities of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say "most of them were issued by the General Staff." Did -- were any issued by any other body or person?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. The war was under -- waged underground. Sometimes communication was not -- did not function properly. So it happened that some communiques were released without the knowledge of the General Staff. It was -- it might have been issued by some operational zones of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific instances where that happened?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. It was not very frequent, but there were some instances when it happened. During the war when some commanders of some zones might have issued communiques on behalf of the zone, but also on behalf of the KLA. But not on behalf of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when that happened, when a commander of a zone issued a communique, would it say that it was -- would it say that it was on behalf of the zone or the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. It said on behalf of the KLA and the zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But if I understand your answer correctly it would not say in those cases that it was on behalf of the General Staff. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus on the communiques that were issued on behalf of the General Staff of the KLA; how were those communicated to the public?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In general initially, because it changed with the passage of time, prior to 1998 in most cases they were faxed or by telephone. But most of them were communicated via fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And they would be faxed to whom?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were faxed mainly to the print media in Albanian, but also to a broader public. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After -- you said prior to 1998 they were faxed or in some instances communicated by telephone. After 1998 how were they communicated?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After or in 1998 they were issued, again via telephone, and international radio stations broadcasting in Albanian. They were sent to radio stations broadcasting in Albanian in Kosova as well. They were sent to the media, whereas from January 1999 when the KLA and the General Staff established the free Kosova and the Kosova Press news agency, all the communiques, all information regarding KLA and what happened on the ground were dispatched through the agency, Kosova Press, via Internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in 1998 you say they were sent to the media. Were they -- did that include the print media, Albanian newspapers?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what newspapers in Albanian, that were published in Albanian, would publish these communiques? And now I'm speaking about 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Bujku, Koha Ditore, and a newspaper that appeared now and again in Switzerland called Zoriko Sor [phoen] and the Bota e Re, New World, which was a bi-monthly or a bi-weekly newspaper of Pristina students.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the communiques that were published in these newspapers that you have just identified that were from the General Staff or said that they were from the General Staff, were they in your -- in fact from the General Staff during 1997 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: To my knowledge with some exception which I don't know of, they were communiques issued by -- on behalf of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So as far as you know every time a communique was published in one of those newspapers that stated it was a communique from the General Staff of the KLA, it was in fact from the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I cannot say that 100 per cent of them were, but in 90 per cent of the cases they were communiques issued by the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in your first answer I understood you to say that there might be an exception that you were not aware of. But now I have understood perhaps you have said something slightly different. Are you aware in 1997 or 1998 of any instance where a communique was published in one of those newspapers in Albanian that you identified and it was not in fact a communique from the General Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Some time, as you know, has passed, but as I said a bulk of them -- I can't rule out that one of them or two may not have been issued directly by the General Staff, but it might have reported on an event without passing through the General Staff. But they are very few I would say, almost insignificant number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And as you sit here today, can you think of any particular instance where that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't recall any such. Also because of the fact that we didn't have time to deal with such communiques that didn't pass through the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to show you some of the communiques and we can talk about each one. I'd ask you, please, with the assistance of the usher and using the large format, if you could look at communique number 35. And it's the ERN on the Albanian version is U008-1607 and the English it's U008-8554. And it will also appear on the Sanction. It's communique 35 in the 8th of August, 1997, published in Koha Ditore on page 3. And I draw your attention to the top left of the page; I believe that's where it appears on the Albanian version. Do you see that communique number 35?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was that communique issued by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the beginning paragraph of the communique, and I'll just read it out. It says: "In a communique for the media bearing number 33, the organisation calling itself 'The Kosova Liberation Army' claims responsibility for recent armed incidents in Kosova, in which two Serbian policemen and two Albanian civilians were injured. This communique states: 'By a decision of the UCK Central Staff made on 3 and 4 August, our guerrilla units carried out three armed operations against the occupiers and the their collaborators.' The organisation also claims responsibility for what we called 'the assassinations of Ali Qullapeku from Terstenik and Ramiz Leku from Baince near Gllogovc [Glogovac]." Do you see that in the communique?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the three armed operations that were referred to that were carried out against the occupiers and their collaborators, did that in fact happen? Were there three armed operations that were carried out?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. As I said earlier, the General Staff had two wings, the political and the operational one. And the communiques were issued mainly by the operational wing, whereas the political statements were issued by the political leaders of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was there communication between the political wing and the operational wing of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the communique also refers to two assassinations of two individuals. Were these two people assassinated because they were suspected of being collaborators?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You must have read several statements and communiques of the KLA and must have seen that the people -- the persons who were the stooges of the Serb regime, who served this violent regime, were drawn attention to some Albanians, who unfortunately were in that position. This was not a common picture of the Albanian population, but the savage regimes, barbarous regimes, at other times in other -- Other European countries have had their collaborators, as is the case with the Second World War, when some French intellectuals and other people joined the collaborationist groups. This happened also in Norway and other countries in Europe. This happened also in Kosova. These people were maybe out of fear and the pressure of the regime obliged to serve this regime. The Kosova Liberation Army has -- constantly has drawn the attention -- has warned such people to withdraw from that activity and not undermine the liberation war. In those cases when the such persons have done great damage to the Albanian people, we have -- as a result of their activity, we have lost many people during the war and many people have been killed in ambushes laid to them. As a result of the activity of such people in those cases the operational wing of the KLA has killed such people because of the service they have rendered to the violent Serb apparatus in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And to your knowledge is that what happened to the two people referenced in this communique, communique 35?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. As the communique said, it must have certainly happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did it happen because they were suspected of being collaborators? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Not because they were suspected, but because they served the occupiers. And even the children of the villages were aware of that in the places where they lived and worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know how it was determined that they were collaborators? How was that decision made? How was it determined?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The decision -- how the decision was made, I don't know; but if they were not in the service of the enemies, if they didn't do any damage to the KLA, such a thing would not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I appreciate your confidence, but my question is: Do you have any information about what the procedure was? Was there any procedure were determining whether these people were collaborators? Was there a trial? Was there a proceeding or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Such persons were not tried in courts because we did not have the conditions for that. But they were executed or killed while they were serving the enemy, as the case has been with the killing of the Serb police and army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think I understand your answer. I'm going to move on to another communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to require the assistance of the usher. This is -- in Albanian -- in the Albanian version it's U008-1608. In the English it's U003-8557 to 8558. It's communique number 40 published on the 5th of December, 1997, in Bujku, on page 10. And I believe on the Albanian version it's in the top right of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to give you a moment to look at that. Is this a communique that was issued by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the first paragraph where it states: "By a decision of the Central Staff, armed units of the UCK continued their liberation operations during November," November, I assume, 1997. "On the evening of 11 November, a hand-grenade attack was carried out against the house of Tomcic, the Serbian-imposed chairman of the commune of Podujeve, in the village of Tashec," and I apologise for my pronunciation, "near Kursumlija, in Operational Zone No. 5. "Our armed units also conducted other liberation operations between 25 and 28 November in Operational Zone No. 1." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were -- did those things that are described in fact occur? Those attacks and operations that are referenced, did those actually occur?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Everything that is said here has really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And there's a reference to Operational Zone Number 5 and Operational Zone Number 1. Where -- first of all, what is operational zone number 1?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Operational Zone Number 1 was in Drenoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Operational Zone Number 5?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was the Llap zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was operational zone 1, did that ever, to your knowledge, did that ever refer to the whole of Kosovo? Or was it always -- did it always refer just to the Drenica zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Drenica zone -- in Kosova there were seven zones, one of them was the Drenica zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But at some time was -- were the seven zones in Kosovo referred to as sub-zones and Kosovo itself referred to as Operational Zone Number 1? Did -- was there ever a time when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, it may have been possible, but the military activity of the KLA was organised in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to draw your attention back to this communique when it refers to Operational Zone Number 1, it -- is it the zone -- the Drenica zone or is it referencing in that case all of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It means the Drenica zone here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to draw your attention now to a sentence which is part-way down -- I would say it's about halfway down and I'll read it out and perhaps you'll be able to find it. "On the evening of 28th November, Dalip Dugolli, a collaborator and one of Milosevic's most trusted men, was killed in the village of Petreshice near Shtime [Stimlje]." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Take your time. I know it's a little -- it's difficult. And I'll read it again. "On the evening of 28th November, Dalip Dugolli," do you see that name, "a collaborator and one of Milosevic's most trusted men, was killed in the village of Petreshice near Shtime [Stimlje]."

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that happen? Did that in fact happen?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. The operational zones in -- given the conditions that prevailed in Kosova, they could act independently on the basis of their own discretion when they had information that some individual who had caused the country damage. They might have undertaken such acts and have notified the General Staff. After that the General Staff has notified the public through the communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with respect to this case - and I'll put to you the same question which I put to you before regarding the previous communique - do you have any information how it was determined that this individual was in fact a collaborator?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I'm telling you again that such acts were undertaken in the conditions of illegality. And the operational units were separated from each other. But they could make their own decisions. When a person was harmful to the KLA, when such a person is giving information on the movements of the KLA to the Belgrade regime, in these instances the unit had all the power of discretion to conduct such acts without any -- without taking the extra approval or supplementary approval for such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand your answer, but I'm just going to ask you again and I'm going to ask your patience with my questions: Do you know if any procedure was followed to determine whether this person was in fact giving information on the movements of the KLA to the Belgrade regime? You've said that trials were not held. But was there any other procedure, any proceeding, that was held? If you know.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: With exception of what I already stated, I don't have anything else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you about another communique and it's -- in the Albanian it's at U008-1610.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- I'm sorry. In the English it's at 8560, U003-8560. It's communique number 42 from the 28th of February, 1998, published in Bujku on page 1. And it appears on the Sanction. And I believe it's in the top middle on the Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was that communique issued from the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of information from the grass roots.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I want to draw your attention to the first sentence of that communique after the introduction and -- where it says: "On the decision of the UCK Central Staff, our armed units undertook a series of attacks against the forces of the Serbian police and their collaborators during January and February." And I'll ask you the same question: Did that in fact occur? Did those attacks occur in January and February?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The attacks have occurred, as the communique says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then about halfway down there's a sentence which says: "On 13 February, 1998, Mustafe Kurti, a collaborator ... was liquidated." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I see not only that sentence but the entire communique issued at that time, and I think that -- you are well-advised to use the whole communique and not take out separate sentences. I am telling again that the KLA has fought against the entire Serb violent operators that has perpetrated genocide and ethnic cleansing in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This apparatus -- please -- couldn't function in Kosova only through its police and soldiers. This apparatus extended its tentacles to all the pores of public administration. They ruled in Kosova also with the help of the collaborators, the people who served the police and the soldiers -- the Serb police and soldiers. That's why I am saying that you are well-advised to look at the communique in all its entirety and not take out names. That is difficult for me to argue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I can assure you that the entire communique is in evidence and will be considered by the Court. I'm just asking you specific questions about specific parts of the communique.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I answered that all those who were in the service of the Milosevic regime and who committed many evils against the Albanian people deserve the same fate that the entire Milosevic regime deserved and had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell me, Mr. Krasniqi, what in your mind is a collaborator? And I know it may seem like a strange question to you, but what is a -- you said "all the people" -- "those who were in the service of the Milosevic regime and committed many evils against the Albanian people." Can you define for us what a collaborator is?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: My belief is that the Honourable Trial Chamber knows very well what a collaborationism is and what collaborators are; this is not a phenomenon typical of Albanians, this is a well-known phenomenon. Back in ancient times if we go into history, this phenomenon has manifested itself, especially during the Second World War and it has manifested itself among all the peoples who have been occupied. Unfortunately, my people had the same destiny. And such people, collaborators, who were numerous, they have received little punishment for what they were. They were in the service in the violent Serb regime. Such people did not deserve a better fate for serving the most criminal regime that has been known by the peoples of Europe after Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I appreciate your answer that the -- collaboration is not unique to this war. But I want you to please try to answer my question, which is: In your mind, and focusing in particular in the war you were involved in, what in your mind was a collaborator? What would -- what are the sorts of things that somebody could do that would make them a collaborator?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I'll give you a concrete example which illustrates my point. On the April the 10th, 1998, in Slatine, 20 kilometres away from Pristina, there is a person was kidnapped. A doctor, humanist doctor, Hafir Shala was kidnapped by the Serb forces. This person has assisted the citizens of Drenoc through humanitarian aid and associations. He has administered his services also to the injured soldiers of the KLA. Because of the people who collaborated with the Milosevic regime, this person was kidnapped and his family knows nothing about his fate. We have many instances like this in Kosova when other persons like Xhavid Haziri, for example, another activist of the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms, it was I think in July, August, he too was kidnapped in Pristina by the Serb secret police because he was spied upon by the collaborators who existed in the war zones when the KLA operated. And I can give you -- such examples are rife.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With respect to that last example, is that July/August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In July, August, and there were also in June, April, even earlier, even before the war. There were many collaborators. Even the case of Likoshan on 28th February, 1998, this came about as a result of the clash between the KLA members and the Serb police, because of the service that the collaborators had done to the Serb police in Drenoc. There are many cases that I know of when collaborators must let the Serb police and soldiers to commit crimes and genocide in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Without this category of bad people, the Belgrade regime wouldn't have been able of living such a long life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you've given now some examples, some specific examples. And I believe earlier you stated that in some instances you believed that collaborators were providing information about the movements of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I will repeat it again and I kindly request the Chamber that the interest on the part of the Prosecution to deal only with these isolated events is very dangerous for the political process in Kosova and does not serve justice and the goal of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, as I told you, the entire communique and other entire communiques are in evidence and considerable evidence about the context of these events has been heard. But for the moment I must focus on these specific questions. With respect to -- still on the subject of collaborators, in some instances were there Albanians who did business, had business, with Serbs who were as a result considered to be collaborators because of their support for the Serb regime? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I understand it very well. Honoured Chamber and Honoured Presiding Judge, the Kosovo Liberation Army which in its second political statement clearly shows its aims and objectives, there were many collaborators in Kosova. And perhaps those that were mentioned here concretely served and damaged the operational units of the Kosovo Liberation Army. However, the KLA did not have as its plan the killing of the citizens of Kosova. But being poor, you actually are experienced with different things. Many people at that time, even today, are in connection with the Serb secret service. However, we did not wage the war against those who collaborated with the Milosevic regime. Our war was mainly directed against the Serb policemen and soldiers. And there when the operational units were at danger, then the killing of those who presented an obstacle took part as well. But the war was mainly directed against those who exercised violence and those who forced people to use their own humanity and honour. In the Political Statement No. 2, which is the KLA programme as presented to the public opinion, it says that "The KLA has a defending and liberating character. Its aim was not war but peace and freedom of its own people. And the KLA will fight on behalf of its people and will self-sacrifice in the name of people. The KLA condemns terrorism and all forms of violence used against civilians. The KLA recognises and abides by the national acts of the United Nations and the Conventions on war," and it goes on. I said -- I focused only on these two points to see or to tell you that the goal of our war was not to attack the collaborators of the enemy who are numerous in Kosova in the economic and the political sphere as well as a cultural and in the security spheres -- the security for Serbia but not for the citizens of Kosova. Therefore, I think that the practice used to try to deck out the Kosova Liberation Army as an army that fought against Albanians and not the Belgrade regime does not serve the truth and has nothing to do with the truth. I do believe that even though the KLA from a guerrilla army was transformed into a popular, voluntary army and at a later phase into an organised army, it did not have as its aim, as its goal, the killing of the people but to win politically over the Serb police and army. Therefore, its victory is also a political victory. Also thanks to the support it had among the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I just want to assure you that certainly nobody on this side of the courtroom, and I'm certain it's true for the other side of the courtroom, is suggesting that the aim of the KLA was primarily to attack Albanians. But we must continue to focus on some of these specific issues. Now, you read out there from a document, and I believe it was Political Statement No. 2. Can you tell us what the date of that is?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: 29th April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I wonder since you read out from that document -- first of all, was that published, that political statement?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was published, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to see where it was published?
